title: Stone Points From Arabia May Have Carried Poison
paragraphs: A paper in the journal Science paints a vivid picture of life on the shore of a freshwater lake that existed in today's Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia roughly 125,000 years ago. Researchers from Griffith University, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and the Saudi Heritage Commission excavated 'Uruq Aljelibah, where more than 5,000 stone artefacts lay among fossils of hippos, buffalo, camels, gazelles and oryx, a reminder that the region was once far greener than it is now.

Under the microscope, several stone points retained animal tissue near the tip and plant resin and fibres at the base, evidence that they were mounted on shafts. Some bore impact damage consistent with hunting large animals, and the spread of tools closely mirrored clusters of bone, suggesting that the lakeshore served as a hub for hunting and butchery. "This suggests people were manufacturing composite weapons made from multiple materials," said lead researcher Christopher Clarkson.

The headline-grabbing detail, however, rests on thinner ground. Chemical biomarkers associated with Acokanthera schimperi, the arrow-poison tree, turned up on several points, raising the possibility of poisoned weapons. The authors stop short of declaring it fact: poison use is inferred, the press release supplies no exact counts, and the dating and sample details are not spelled out there. Until further work firms up the case, it remains a tantalising hypothesis rather than a settled discovery.

questions.q: What does the mix of animal fossils and tools suggest about the region?
questions.a: It was once much greener, with a lake.

questions.q: What did the pattern of tools and bones suggest?
questions.a: The shore was a hub for hunting and processing game.

questions.q: Why is the poison finding described as thin?
questions.a: It is inferred from chemical traces, with no exact counts given.
